strengths: Originality/significance: CGP is a useful combination of layer-wise convex aggregation and prototype-based patch-token probing. BAT also offers a practically relevant modernization of an aging audio SSL pipeline.

Soundness: The method is mathematically specified, and the comparisons consistently show that CGP substantially outperforms both final-layer linear probing and Protobin on EAT and SSLAM. BAT improves frozen-feature results across all four evaluated datasets.

The layer-wise probe results provide an interesting diagnostic: replacing the CNN decoder with a ViT decoder shifts useful information toward later encoder blocks, suggesting a plausible relationship between decoder capacity and representation quality.

Presentation is generally clear, with readable figures, cumulative ablations, dataset/resource summaries, and hyperparameter tables. The paper is also commendably candid that prior reported fine-tuning results could not be fully reproduced and that later-layer dominance should not be treated as universal.
The work uses established public benchmarks and identifies no unusual ethical risk; frozen evaluation could reduce downstream computational cost.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that CGP is a "faithful" evaluator is not established. Closeness to fine-tuning performance does not demonstrate faithfulness to intrinsic representation quality. There is no evaluation of ranking reliability across many models, correlation with transfer performance, robustness to distribution shift, or resistance to label fitting.

CGP is considerably more expressive than the framing suggests. With 10,000 prototypes, a ViT-Base probe has roughly 7.7M prototype parameters, plus an AudioSet classifier from 30,000 features to 527 labels (about 15.8M parameters). This capacity may explain much of the gain over simpler probes, but parameter counts, compute, memory, and capacity-matched baselines are not reported.

The "new SOTA" claim is overstated. BAT reaches 48.55 mAP on AS-2M versus SSLAM's reported 50.2 and 95.52 on ESC-50 versus the reported 96.2; it mainly surpasses the authors' own reproductions under their protocol. That is useful evidence for a controlled baseline, but not a general benchmark SOTA.

All main results are single numbers without multiple seeds, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. This is especially problematic for small datasets and for small ablation differences such as 34.86 to 35.03 mAP. The paper attributes discrepancies to optimization instability while not quantifying its own run-to-run variability.

The BAT ablations are cumulative, conducted only on AS-20k with CGP, and do not verify each component under linear probing and fine-tuning. Thus the model changes and the proposed evaluator are partly entangled. The substantially heavier ViT decoder also lacks a compute-matched comparison or reporting of pretraining cost.

The attention-sink explanation is supported mainly by one qualitative attention visualization. No quantitative sink/sparsity metric, controlled alternative gating design, or collapse/stability analysis establishes the proposed mechanism.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for a paper whose central motivation is reproducibility. Code and weights are only promised after acceptance or on request, and important implementation details are missing, including complete frontend parameters, mask construction, EMA schedule, architecture configuration, initialization, model-selection procedure, and dataset snapshot. AudioSet availability differences are acknowledged as a possible cause but not controlled.

The ESC-50 protocol appears to use a 1,600/400 split, whereas standard reporting generally averages five folds; the manuscript does not clarify fold selection or aggregation. Metric naming is also unclear across multiclass tasks, and Figure 6 labels its vertical axis as mAP. These ambiguities weaken comparability.

Presentation has several correctness issues: CGP is repeatedly called "CGB" in related work, Data2Vec appears as duplicated references, and BYOL is cited as a 2025 NeurIPS work. The impact statement is also too cursory: general audio representation models can implicate privacy, surveillance, dataset bias, and consent even if this work introduces no unique acute risk.

strengths: Soundness: CGP is clearly specified mathematically, and Table 1 demonstrates large gains over both linear probing and Protobin on EAT and SSLAM. The gated-target experiment is a useful 2×2 ablation, while the decoder experiment yields a substantial AS-20k improvement. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/2c31a04eaa5e4f9bb4a215b2259db95f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Significance: More reliable frozen evaluation of audio representations is an important problem, and the reproduced-versus-reported results usefully draw attention to sensitivity in current AudioSet evaluation pipelines.
Presentation: The main method, experimental progression, and headline comparisons are generally easy to follow. Figures 1 and 4 communicate the layer aggregation and layer-wise behavior effectively.

Originality: Combining prototype-based patch aggregation with learned convex layer mixing is a sensible extension, and the resulting frozen-feature performance is practically promising. BAT also offers a potentially useful consolidated PyTorch implementation of several modernization choices.
The paper reports multiple evaluation modes—fine-tuning, CGP, and linear probing—on four datasets, rather than relying on a single downstream result.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that CGP is a “faithful,” “robust,” or reliable measure of intrinsic representation quality is not established. Closing the accuracy gap to fine-tuning does not validate faithfulness, and there is no analysis of ranking stability across seeds, hyperparameters, data regimes, or broader model families.

CGP is a high-capacity supervised head rather than a lightweight probe: with 10,000 prototypes and 768-dimensional features, the prototypes alone add about 7.7M parameters; on AudioSet, the 30,000-to-527 classifier adds about 15.8M more. This capacity, plus nonlinear min/max aggregation over patches, complicates comparisons with linear probing and undermines the parameter-efficiency framing. Training cost, memory, and inference cost are not reported.

The CGP contribution is insufficiently isolated. There are no ablations separating layer gating, intermediate features, the CLS branch, minimum pooling, maximum pooling, and prototype count. Comparisons are limited mainly to Protobin and a linear probe, omitting relevant intermediate-feature adaptation methods discussed in related work.

The paper makes mechanistic claims that exceed its evidence. A single qualitative attention map does not show that gating removes attention sinks or that noisy MHSA dependencies cause inferior targets. Likewise, “strong correlation” between gating weights and per-layer probe quality is asserted visually without coefficients, uncertainty, or tests across tasks and seeds.

The empirical results contain no repeated runs, error bars, statistical tests, or sensitivity analysis. Several claimed gains are small—for example, +0.17 mAP for preprocessing and +0.09 mAP for the larger ViT decoder—and could readily lie within run-to-run variation. This is particularly problematic for a paper centered on unreliability and reproducibility.

The “new SOTA on audio benchmarks” claim is inaccurate or at least seriously overstated. BAT exceeds reported fine-tuning results only on AS-20k; its AS-2M score of 48.55 is below SSLAM’s reported 50.2, its ESC-50 score of 95.52 is below 96.2, and its SC-2 score of 98.13 is below 98.3. Frozen-probe results are not directly comparable to prior fine-tuning SOTA.

The claim that prior gains arise from “optimization artifacts or dataset differences” is speculative. Failure to reproduce selected reported numbers under the authors’ framework does not identify the cause, especially without multiple seeds, systematic hyperparameter sweeps, or a controlled comparison against the original code. EAT is in fact reproduced closely on AS-20k.

BAT bundles frontend changes, gated attention, altered targets, removal of loss scaling, bfloat16 training, and a much stronger decoder. The cumulative, mostly single-run ablation does not fully disentangle these changes or control for added parameters and pretraining computation, weakening causal attribution and fairness of the baseline comparison.

Originality is moderate: CGP appears to add a global scalar layer mixture to an existing prototype probe, while BAT largely combines known frontend processing, gated attention transferred from LLMs, and the established use of a stronger ViT decoder. The paper does not demonstrate a deeper new principle beyond this integration.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite being a central selling point. Code is unavailable at review time, and the appendix omits seeds, variance, checkpoint-selection rules, exact frontend and masking parameters, EMA schedule, full architecture details, ESC-50 fold protocol, thresholding for F1, and sufficient implementation detail for CGP. Stating that code will be released upon acceptance does not support present verification.

Presentation needs greater precision: CGP is repeatedly called “CGB,” mAP is described as accuracy, “min-max pooling” could be confused with min-max normalization, and there are citation/reference anomalies such as BYOL being dated 2025 and duplicated Data2Vec entries. The manuscript also lacks a candid limitations section.

Ethics and limitations are treated superficially. Audio models can implicate privacy, surveillance, consent, and demographic or geographic dataset bias, yet the impact statement declares no specific negative consequences. The claimed carbon benefit is also unsupported by compute or emissions measurements despite 400k-step, multi-A100 pretraining.

strengths: Soundness: The central empirical result is substantial: on AS-20k, CGP raises EAT from 17.95 linear-probe mAP and 31.22 Protobin mAP to 35.20, while BAT reaches 37.52. The factorial target/gating ablation in Table 3 and decoder study in Table 4 provide useful evidence for the architectural choices.

Significance: Improving frozen evaluation for audio SSL is valuable because fine-tuning can confound representation quality. The contrasting rankings of EAT and SSLAM under reported fine-tuning, reproduced fine-tuning, and frozen probing illustrate this problem concretely.

Evaluation breadth: BAT is evaluated with fine-tuning, CGP, and linear probing on AS-2M, AS-20k, ESC-50, and Speech Commands V2. It consistently improves over the authors' standardized EAT/SSLAM reproductions in the principal CGP comparisons.

Originality: CGP is a simple, useful synthesis of prototype-based spatial aggregation and a learned convex mixture over encoder layers. BAT combines this evaluation tool with a modernized audio SSL pipeline, gated attention targets, and a stronger decoder.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. Equations 8–11 specify CGP compactly, and Figures 4–6 make the layer-distribution interpretation accessible. weaknesses: Soundness: The strong characterization of CGP as a “faithful” and robust evaluator is not established. There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, sensitivity analyses, ranking correlations across a broader model collection, or evidence that CGP rankings better predict transfer than alternative probes.

CGP is a comparatively high-capacity supervised probe: 10,000 learned D-dimensional prototypes, min/max nonlinear aggregation, and a classifier. The paper does not report its parameter count, compute, memory, sample efficiency, or overfitting behavior. Comparisons are limited mainly to linear probing and Protobin rather than other layer-aware or attentive adaptation methods discussed in Section 2.

The claim that CGP “drastically closes” the fine-tuning gap is metric-dependent. For EAT on AS-2M, CGP obtains 41.04 versus 47.61 mAP, but only 19.51 versus 36.63 F1. This large F1 discrepancy is neither analyzed nor reconciled with the headline claim.

The broad “new SOTA on audio benchmarks” language is overstated. BAT exceeds the reproduced baselines, but its fine-tuned results remain below reported SSLAM on AS-2M (48.55 versus 50.2), ESC-50 (95.52 versus 96.2), and reported EAT on SC-2 (98.13 versus 98.3). Only the AS-20k fine-tuning result clearly exceeds the reported values.

Several mechanistic conclusions exceed the evidence. The claim that gating removes attention sinks rests largely on a single qualitative attention visualization, while the claim that the ViT decoder offloads reconstruction and shifts semantics is supported by correlations rather than a direct causal analysis. Learned gating weights are also treated as information-location measurements without testing their stability or faithfulness.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite being a central theme. Code and pretrained weights are not included with the submission; exact frontend/STFT parameters, EMA schedule, masking details, prototype initialization, and CGP training procedure are insufficiently specified. There are also inconsistencies between the main text and Appendix A, including batch size 48 versus 12 and warm-up of 50k versus 53k steps.

The limitations discussion is too brief. It mentions future domain and scaling evaluations but not single-run uncertainty, dependence on 10,000 prototypes, substantial pretraining compute, the narrow baseline set, or possible dataset-specific behavior. The impact statement also dismisses negative consequences without discussing privacy, demographic bias, or surveillance risks associated with models trained on large-scale audio containing human speech.

Originality is useful but moderate: scalar layer mixing and prototype probing both have close precedents, while gated attention, stronger decoders, and frontend changes are imported or adapted from prior work. Minor presentation issues include inconsistent use of CGP/CGB, an erroneous “mAP” axis for gating weights in Figure 6, and incorrect or duplicated bibliographic entries such as BYOL dated 2025.

strengths: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem in audio self-supervised learning: downstream finetuning can confound representation quality, while last-layer linear probing can substantially underestimate token-based audio representations.

The empirical scope is strong. BAT, EAT, SSLAM, and BEATs are compared across AudioSet, ESC-50, Speech Commands, sound-event detection, out-of-distribution bird classification, and LibriSpeech ASR, using several adaptation protocols. BAT consistently performs well and often leads within each protocol.

CGP is simple and practically motivated: it learns a convex combination of layers, preserves patch-level information through prototype similarities, and combines minimum, maximum, and class-token statistics. The computational analysis reports parameters, memory, latency, and MACs rather than presenting accuracy alone.

The BAT ablations form a reasonably coherent development path. The frontend change gives a small improvement, gated attention combined with end-of-block targets improves further, and replacing the CNN decoder with a ViT decoder provides the largest reported gain. The layer-weight plots offer useful qualitative insight into where downstream information resides.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The method is mathematically specified, major hyperparameters and dataset sizes are tabulated, and the authors appropriately acknowledge that later-layer concentration is not universally evidence of a better representation.

The work has useful practical significance even though many ingredients are adaptations: it modernizes a difficult-to-reproduce audio SSL pipeline and reports failures to reproduce published EAT/SSLAM finetuning results rather than concealing them.
weaknesses: The central claim that CGP is a “faithful” or “reliable” measure of intrinsic representation quality is not established. Closing the numerical gap to finetuning and producing similar rankings over only four models does not validate faithfulness. CGP is itself a high-capacity supervised learner with 10,000 prototypes and 23.49M trainable parameters, so improved downstream accuracy may reflect probe capacity rather than better extraction of information already readily available in the representation. No controlled-capacity comparison, label-efficiency study, synthetic ground-truth test, or correlation across a sufficiently large and diverse model population is provided.

Model and probe development appears to use benchmark test results directly. The paper states that all ablations are conducted on AS-20k, whose dataset table lists no validation split, and repeatedly selects frontend, target, attention, decoder, prototype count, loss, and “refined hyperparameters” from these results. Unless an unreported held-out development split was used, the final AS-20k SOTA comparison is test-contaminated. Comparable tuning protocols for the remaining benchmarks are also unspecified.

Statistical evidence is inadequate for many decisive comparisons. Most AudioSet, Speech Commands, SED, HSN, and ASR entries are single values without seed variability or significance analysis. Several claimed gains are small—for example, the frontend changes mAP from 34.86 to 35.03 and gated attention with MLP targets from 35.03 to 35.09—so these results cannot support causal conclusions without repeated trials.

The mechanistic explanation is stronger than the evidence. The claim that ungated attention introduces degenerate dependencies or attention sinks that corrupt SSL targets is supported mainly by a qualitative attention visualization. Likewise, the decoder interpretation and claimed correlation between CGP weights and per-layer linear performance lack quantitative controls or correlation statistics. Multiple changes are combined when comparing the final BAT with EAT.

The SOTA framing is overstated. BAT does not exceed the reported SSLAM result on AS-2M (48.85 versus 50.2 mAP), even though the paper disputes that baseline's reproducibility, and its advances largely combine known components: local spectrogram normalization, previously proposed sigmoid-gated attention, and the established use of a stronger ViT decoder. The audio-specific integration is useful, but methodological originality is moderate.

Fairness among probing methods is unclear. A single shared optimization recipe need not be appropriate for structurally different probes, CGP benefits from substantially more parameters than LP, LCGP, H2T, and Protobin, and only limited method-specific tuning is reported. The claim that CGP “significantly outperforms” alternatives is made without statistical testing.

Reproducibility is improved by the hyperparameter, resource, and latency tables, but important details remain dependent on promised code: model/decoder configuration details, data-sampling behavior, augmentation implementation, checkpoint selection, random seeds, thresholding for F1, and hyperparameter-search ranges are not fully specified. The manuscript's code-availability field is blank in the supplied PDF, so the claimed implementation cannot be assessed here.

The impact statement is cursory. Audio representation models can implicate privacy, surveillance, demographic/domain bias, and dataset licensing concerns; claiming no specific negative consequences without discussing these issues is incomplete, although the experiments use established public benchmarks and no acute ethical violation is evident.

strengths: The manuscript presents a substantial empirical study, with a clearly described probe, sequential BAT ablations, comparisons against several adaptation methods, and downstream evaluation spanning classification, OOD recognition, sound-event detection, and speech recognition. Soundness: The BAT results are generally consistent across adaptation protocols. In Table 5, BAT outperforms EAT and SSLAM under finetuning, CGP, PB, VQT, and H2T on most tasks; the decoder ablation also produces a meaningful AS-20k gain from 35.42 to 37.52 mAP.

Presentation: The paper is organized well, explains the masked-latent-regression setup and CGP equations clearly, and provides useful architecture diagrams, hyperparameter tables, dataset summaries, and probing-cost measurements.

Significance: The difficulty reproducing published EAT and SSLAM finetuning results is potentially important for the audio-SSL community. Providing a modern PyTorch implementation and broader standardized evaluation could be practically valuable.

Originality: Although its ingredients are largely established, combining prototype-based token aggregation with a learned convex mixture of layers is a sensible extension. Using the learned mixture to inspect where task-relevant information resides is also useful.
The paper includes a welcome caveat that later-layer concentration is not universally evidence of a better representation, rather than presenting this diagnostic as a general law.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that CGP is a faithful or reliable measure of representation quality is not established by showing that it attains higher downstream accuracy or approaches finetuning. CGP is itself a powerful supervised learner with 10,000 trainable prototypes, nonlinear cosine features, min/max token pooling, and 23.49M parameters. It could learn substantial task structure rather than merely expose information already accessible in the representation. The paper lacks parameter-matched nonlinear probes, label-efficiency curves, frozen/random-backbone controls, or other tests that distinguish probe expressivity from representation quality.

The claimed reliability is further weakened by sensitivity within the paper: EAT's AS-2M CGP mAP changes from 41.04 in Table 1 to 42.98 in Table 5 after using refined hyperparameters and asymmetric loss. Most AudioSet results are single runs without uncertainty, statistical tests, or sensitivity analyses. Consequently, terms such as 'significantly,' 'robust,' and 'default evaluation paradigm' are not adequately supported.

The BAT analysis bundles several known interventions and often overinterprets small ablations. The claim that gating fixes attention sinks rests mainly on qualitative heatmaps; no quantitative sink statistic or parameter-matched control is provided. With gating, changing MLP targets to EOB targets improves mAP by only 0.33 without error bars. Likewise, the frontend gain is only 0.17 mAP, yet the text asserts better signal integrity, noise suppression, robustness, and faster training without measurements supporting those properties.

The decoder result is promising, but the comparison is not controlled for parameter count or pretraining compute: a six-layer CNN is replaced by a much larger six-layer ViT. A widened/deeper CNN or other compute-matched decoder is needed before attributing the improvement specifically to decoder form or reconstruction offloading. Pretraining latency, FLOPs, energy, and total GPU-hours are also absent, despite efficiency and carbon-footprint claims.

Significance and originality are overstated. CGP largely combines the prior ProtoBin mechanism with the familiar learned weighted sum of intermediate layers. BAT combines an alternative frontend, gated attention imported from prior LLM work, EOB targets, and the already established finding that stronger MAE decoders can improve encoders. This is a useful engineering synthesis, but not a strongly novel algorithmic contribution.

The state-of-the-art language is imprecise. BAT's reproduced results exceed the authors' reproduced baselines, but its AS-2M finetuning mAP of 48.85 remains below SSLAM's reported 50.2. Failure to reproduce a published number is valuable evidence of fragility, but does not by itself invalidate that number or establish a new SOTA. Conclusions should distinguish reproduced-comparison wins from wins over reported results.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite being a central theme. The appendix gives many optimization hyperparameters, but omits important implementation-level details such as the full spectrogram configuration, gate/prototype initialization, thresholding used for F1, exact model dimensions, and complete sampling procedure. The displayed code link is blank in the submitted manuscript, and there is no independent rerun or multi-seed pretraining evidence. Stating that results matched across devices is not a substitute for an externally verifiable artifact.

Presentation is generally strong, but Table 5 is extremely dense and difficult to read. Several conclusions blur representation quality, probe accuracy, and linear separability, which should be treated as distinct concepts.

Limitations and ethics are treated too briefly. The paper acknowledges one interpretive limitation but does not adequately discuss the probe-capacity confound, computational cost of storing all-layer features, dependence on AudioSet pretraining, or limited pretraining replication. The impact statement's assertion of no unique negative consequences overlooks privacy, surveillance, demographic/domain bias, dataset licensing, and misuse considerations relevant to large-scale audio and speech models. These concerns are not necessarily prohibitive, but they should be addressed.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical results are broad and internally consistent. CGP substantially outperforms linear probing, Head2Toe, VQT, and ProtoBin across AudioSet, ESC-50, Speech Commands, sound-event detection, and an out-of-distribution bird-audio task. BAT also consistently improves over EAT, SSLAM, and BEATs under several adaptation protocols, reducing the chance that its advantage is peculiar to one probe.

The ablation sequence is informative: the frontend, gated attention and target choice, and decoder capacity are introduced separately. In particular, the interaction in Table 3—end-of-block targets hurt without gating but help with gating—is useful evidence for the proposed design, while Table 4 shows that the expressive decoder is the largest contributor.

Significance: Exposing reproducibility problems in AudioSet finetuning and providing a stronger frozen-feature evaluation protocol addresses an important practical weakness in audio SSL. The inclusion of classification, dense detection, domain shift, and speech recognition gives the work considerably broader value than another AudioSet-only model comparison.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and unusually transparent about failed reproductions, sensitive regularization, and the fact that later-layer concentration is not universally a measure of representation quality. Figures 1 and 4 communicate the method and layer analysis effectively.

Originality: CGP is a useful combination of learned convex layer aggregation with prototype similarities and min/max token pooling. Although its ingredients are related to existing layer weighting and prototypical probes, their integration for multi-label audio evaluation is novel and practically effective.

Reproducibility: The appendix reports optimizer settings, schedules, batch sizes, augmentation choices, losses, dataset splits, probe sizes, hardware, and computational costs. A native PyTorch reimplementation of legacy pipelines and the stated release of baseline evaluation code would be valuable community infrastructure.
weaknesses: The central description of CGP as a “faithful” measure of inherent representation quality is not fully established. CGP is itself a high-capacity supervised adapter with 23.49M trainable parameters and 10,000 prototypes; closing the gap to finetuning can reflect adapter expressiveness rather than more faithful measurement. The paper does not test probe rankings against an independent criterion such as label efficiency, transfer to unseen tasks, robustness across probe hyperparameters, or controlled representations of known quality.

Comparisons among probes are not capacity- or compute-matched. CGP is much larger than the linear and Head2Toe probes, and Table 10 appears to compare operations on pre-extracted all-layer features against VQT operating through the backbone. Feature-extraction time and the storage cost of all patch tokens from all layers are omitted, weakening the efficiency claim.

Several mechanistic claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper attributes the improvement from gating to removal of attention sinks and interprets the heavier decoder as offloading low-level reconstruction, but provides mainly downstream correlations and qualitative attention maps. Quantitative attention-sink statistics, reconstruction analyses, or interventions isolating the proposed mechanisms are missing.

The strongest BAT improvements combine known or imported techniques: local frontend normalization, gated attention adapted from LLMs, end-of-block targets, and a larger ViT decoder motivated by MAE. This is a useful synthesis, but the architectural originality is moderate. Moreover, increased decoder capacity introduces a pretraining-compute confound that is not quantified.

Uncertainty reporting is inadequate for the main claims. Most AudioSet results and all major pretraining ablations appear to come from single runs, despite small gains such as 0.17 mAP for the frontend and 0.39 mAP for gated attention with MLP targets. Error bars are reported only for ESC-50, and there are no significance or seed-stability analyses for CGP rankings.

The “new SOTA” wording is too broad. BAT exceeds the reproduced baselines and the reported AS-20k results, but its AS-2M finetuning result (48.85 mAP) remains below SSLAM’s reported 50.2. For the other datasets, the table compares only the selected pretrained backbones rather than the wider task-specific state of the art.

The inability to reproduce EAT and SSLAM is important, but it does not by itself establish that their reported improvements are optimization artifacts. Changes in available AudioSet clips, sampling, software, or unreported details could contribute. A more controlled sensitivity study would better substantiate this conclusion.

Although hyperparameters are extensive, key reproducibility details are deferred to code, including the sampler identified as crucial; the supplied manuscript displays no usable code URL. Exact frontend parameters, total GPU-hours, run counts, and variability across seeds are also missing.

The impact statement is overly categorical in claiming no specific negative ethical consequences. General-purpose audio representations can support privacy-invasive recording, surveillance, and performance disparities across languages, speakers, environments, or species; these risks merit at least brief acknowledgment.
